text: ZAAL vs GERMS. Level 1 , The Bleeding Ulcer. Zaal has shrunk down smaller than a grain of sand and flown all the way into a person's stomach! The stomach is a stretchy bag in your belly. It squishes up your food and mixes it with strong acid to break it into tiny bits. That's called digesting.

Uh-oh. What went wrong? The stomach protects itself with a thick coat of slime called mucus, a bit like snot. The slime stops the acid from burning the stomach wall. But corkscrew-shaped germs called H. pylori drilled through the slime, like tiny screwdrivers. With no slime to protect it, the acid burned a sore into the stomach wall. A sore like this is called an ulcer.

Now it's bleeding! The ulcer went so deep that it broke open a tiny blood vessel, one of the tubes that carry blood around your body. Now red blood cells are spilling out into the stomach! Red blood cells are your body's delivery drivers. They carry oxygen, the part of the air you breathe in, to every part of you. You can't live without it. If they stay in the stomach, the acid will digest them just like food. They have to get back into the blood through a vein. And the acid is starting to rise.

Meet your team. 1 , ZaalThe explorer. He can super-jump. He can also zap a nerve (one of the body's message wires) to open a valve, a little door inside the vein. 2 , GobblerA macrophage , a big white blood cell. White blood cells are your body's army against germs. Gobbler swallows germs whole! 3 , PatchA platelet , a tiny bit of a cell in your blood. Platelets stick together to plug leaks with a clot. Patch builds clot bridges.

Your mission. Get at least 7 of the 10 red blood cells into the vein, and all 3 heroes too. Blood cells walk all by themselves. They turn around when they bump into a hero, so a hero standing still is a wall. The blood cells wait in the torn vessel until you press R. Clear the way first! Every power needs a maths problem. Stuck? Press Show me how. After a while the acid starts to rise, so don't hang around!
This is a person, a lot like you. Inside are lots of organs: body parts that each have a special job. Somewhere in here, germs are causing trouble!
Zaal jumps into his tiny ship, shrinks smaller than a grain of sand, and flies in through the mouth!
Down the food pipe! Its proper name is the oesophagus . Its muscles squeeze food down to the stomach.
Splash! This is the stomach. It sits on the left side of the belly (on your right as you look at them), tucked just under the ribs.
Zoom in close to the stomach wall. Uh-oh. Something is very wrong down here!
Body fact! An ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach. Lots of them are caused by the germ H. pylori.
Body fact! H. pylori is spiral-shaped. It spins like a corkscrew to drill into the stomach's slimy mucus.
Body fact! Acid can't easily kill H. pylori: it makes a cloud of ammonia around itself as a shield!
Body fact! Barry Marshall drank a cup of H. pylori to prove it makes stomachs sick. He and Robin Warren won a Nobel Prize in 2005.
Body fact! Macrophage means "big eater" in Greek. They swallow germs whole and digest them inside.
Body fact! Bacteria multiply by splitting in two. Some kinds can double every 20 minutes!
Body fact! Platelets aren't whole cells. They're tiny fragments that stick together to plug leaks.
Body fact! Platelets make a plug, then a stringy protein called fibrin weaves a net over it. That's a clot!
Body fact! Veins have little valves inside them, like doors, so blood can't flow backwards.
Body fact! Nerve signals are electrical. The fastest ones travel over 100 metres per second!
Body fact! Red blood cells have no nucleus. That leaves more room for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.
Body fact! A red blood cell lives about 120 days. A grown-up has about 25 trillion of them!
Body fact! Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid. It's strong enough to dissolve some metals!
Body fact! Your stomach coats itself in thick mucus so it doesn't digest itself.
Your secret code is P, L, O, P. PLOP!

ZAAL vs GERMS. Level 2 , The Great Poo Escape. Remember the person whose stomach ulcer we fixed? Their tummy feels much better. But now it's gurgling, and they keep running to the toilet! Zaal has flown further down the gut, into the large intestine. Its other name is the colon . It's the last part of the gut, where poo is made.

What went wrong? Your colon is home to trillions of good bacteria. They help break down food, and they fill up all the space so bad germs can't move in. All the tiny living things in your gut together are called your microbiome. Last week the person had a bad ear infection, so the doctor gave them antibiotics: medicine that kills bacteria. The antibiotics killed the germs in the ear. but they also wiped out loads of the good bacteria in the gut. Oops!

A bully moves in. With the good bacteria gone, a nasty germ called C. diff moved into the empty space. It makes toxins, which are poisons. They hurt the colon wall and cause diarrhoea: very, very runny poo. C. diff has a sneaky trick. When it's in danger, it turns into a spore: a tough, armoured shell that's really hard to destroy. Everything down here is SLOPPY. And the smell! Pee-yew!

The cure: a poo transplant! Doctors have a real cure for this, and it's brilliantly gross. It's called a poo transplant: good bacteria from a healthy person's poo are put into the poorly person's gut. The bacteria can even come in pills. Their real nickname is "crapsules"! (Don't worry, they're sealed and clean.). A crapsule has just landed in the colon with 10 good bacteria inside. They need to reach the bare colon wall and move in, so there's no room left for C. diff.

Meet your team. 1 , ZaalThe explorer. He can super-jump, and he can zap a nerve to open a sphincter : a ring of muscle that squeezes shut. 2 , GobblerOur hungry macrophage. He swallows C. diff. But if one turns into a spore, it's too tough for him! 3 , GobletNew! A goblet cell, shaped like a wine glass. She squirts mucus: slime for poo boulders and mucus rafts across the swamp. Patch stayed behind in the stomach to keep the ulcer patched up.

Your mission. Get at least 7 of the 10 good bacteria to the bare pink wall. Then get all 3 heroes out through the rectum. Good bacteria walk by themselves. A hero standing still is a wall that turns them around. If a bacterium falls in the swamp or gets bullied by C. diff, it pops back into the crapsule for another go. No rush! Gas vents float you up. Yes, they're farts. Squishy poo sinks if you stand still on it. Keep moving! Now and then a big peristalsis squeeze rolls by. It makes everyone hop and sweeps spores away.
Back to our person! We fixed their stomach ulcer, but now their tummy is gurgling and they keep running to the toilet. Something is wrong further down.
Zaal's tiny ship zooms back down into the stomach.
.and on into the small intestine: a long, thin tube about 6 metres long, all coiled up! It's lined with millions of tiny fingers called villi , like a fluffy carpet.
Into the large intestine! That little dead-end tube is the appendix. It's on the person's right side, so it's on our left as we look at them.
Up, then across the top. The large intestine is also called the colon. It's wide, and about 1.5 metres long.
Zoom in close. Uh-oh. It is VERY runny down here. And what is that SMELL?!
Zaal zaps the outer sphincter, and. BOMBS AWAY!
PLOP! A perfect Type 4: smooth and soft, like a sausage. With the good bacteria back, the colon makes proper poo again!
Somebody pulls the flush. WHOOOOOSH!
Wheee! Round the U-bend, with the C. diff spores tumbling after. Bye bye, germs!
One last thing: always wash your hands with soap and water after the toilet. Hand gel can't kill C. diff spores, but soap washes them away!
Body fact! Antibiotics kill bacteria. They can't tell good gut bacteria from bad germs, so they often wipe out both.
Body fact! Poo-transplant pills have a real nickname: "crapsules"!
Body fact! A poo transplant puts good bacteria from a healthy person's poo into a poorly gut. It cures most C. diff infections that keep coming back.
Body fact! C. diff is short for Clostridioides difficile. "Difficile" means difficult, because it was so hard to grow in a lab!
Body fact! C. diff makes toxins that damage the colon wall. That's what causes the runny diarrhoea.
Body fact! C. diff is rod-shaped. When it makes a spore, it bulges at one end like a drumstick!
Body fact! Your gut is home to about 38 trillion bacteria. That's about as many as all the cells in the rest of your body!
Body fact! In danger, C. diff turns into a spore: a tough armoured shell. Spores can survive for months on things like door handles.
Body fact! Spores wake up and turn back into germs when they sense bile, a juice from your liver, in the gut.
Body fact! C. diff spores leave the body in poo. That's how they spread, so always wash your hands after the toilet!
Body fact! Poo is about 75% water. The colon soaks water back out, which is why poo gets firmer as it travels along.
Body fact! Up to about half of the solid part of poo is bacteria, alive and dead!
Body fact! Poo is brown because of old red blood cells! Their haemoglobin becomes bilirubin, then gut bacteria turn it into brown stercobilin.
Body fact! Most people fart about 15 times a day. Most of the gas has no smell at all. The stinky part is less than 1%!
Body fact! Fart gas is mostly nitrogen from swallowed air, plus hydrogen, carbon dioxide and sometimes methane made by gut bacteria.
Body fact! Poo smells because gut bacteria make stinky chemicals called skatole and indole.
Body fact! Muscles in your gut squeeze in waves to push food and poo along. That's peristalsis. It works even if you're upside down!
Body fact! Lots of good bacteria hold on to the gut with tiny hairs called pili (say "PIE-lie"). That's how they don't get swept away.
Body fact! Goblet cells are shaped like a wine glass. They squirt out mucus so poo slides along smoothly.
Body fact! Your colon is about 1.5 metres long. The small intestine is about 6 metres long, but much thinner!
Body fact! You have two sphincters at the very end. The inner one works all by itself. The outer one is the one you control!
Body fact! Doctors use the Bristol Stool Chart to describe poo. It has 7 types, from hard lumps (Type 1) to watery (Type 7).
Brain says: Was that a rumble down there?
Brain says: Hmm. We might need a toilet soon.
Brain says: We need a toilet SOON!
Brain says: FIND A TOILET! I'm crossing my legs up here!
Brain says: Seriously. Toilet. NOW. Please?
Brain says: Pardon me! Was that you down there?
Brain says: Hold it! We haven't found a toilet yet!
Brain says: TOILET FOUND! Sitting down now. Zaal, zap the nerve to open the way out!
Brain says: Ready. steady. PUSH! Everybody out!
Your secret code is B, U, R, P. BURP!
stomach. A stretchy bag in your belly. It squishes food and mixes it with acid.
acid. A strong liquid that breaks things down. Stomach acid helps digest food.
digest. To break food down into tiny bits your body can use.
mucus. Thick slime, a bit like snot. It coats the stomach so the acid can't burn it.
germ. A tiny living thing that can make you ill. Far too small to see without a microscope.
bacteria. One kind of germ. Each one is just a single tiny cell.
H. pylori. A corkscrew-shaped bacterium that lives in stomachs and can cause ulcers.
ulcer. A sore in the stomach wall, where the acid has burned through.
cell. The tiny building blocks your body is made of. You have trillions of them!
blood vessel. A tube that carries blood around your body.
vein. A blood vessel that carries blood back to your heart.
valve. A little door inside a vein. It only lets blood flow one way.
nerve. A body wire that carries messages between your brain and the rest of you.
red blood cell. A cell that carries oxygen around your body. Millions of them make blood red.
oxygen. The part of the air your body needs to live. You breathe it in.
white blood cell. A germ-fighting cell. White blood cells are your body's army.
macrophage. A big white blood cell that swallows germs whole. The name means "big eater".
platelet. A tiny piece of a cell in your blood. Platelets stick together to plug leaks.
clot. A sticky plug made of platelets and stringy fibrin that stops bleeding. A scab is a dried clot!
fibrin. A stringy protein that weaves a net over a platelet plug to make it strong.
organ. A body part with a special job, like your heart, lungs or stomach.
oesophagus. The food pipe. A muscly tube that squeezes food down from your mouth to your stomach.
liver. A big organ next to your stomach. It cleans your blood and helps digest fat.
immune system. All the parts of your body that fight germs.
colon. The large intestine: the last part of your gut, where poo is made.
large intestine. The wide tube at the end of your gut. It soaks water out of poo. Its other name is the colon.
small intestine. A long, thin tube after the stomach. Most of your food gets soaked into your blood here.
villi. Millions of tiny finger shapes lining the small intestine, like a fluffy carpet.
appendix. A small dead-end tube that sticks out of the large intestine.
microbiome. All the tiny living things that live in and on your body.
antibiotic. A medicine that kills bacteria. It can't kill viruses, like the ones that give you colds.
C. diff. Short for Clostridioides difficile. A germ that can take over the gut and cause bad diarrhoea.
toxin. A poison made by a living thing, like a germ.
diarrhoea. Very runny poo.
spore. A germ inside a tough armoured shell. It can sleep for months and wake up later.
poo transplant. Putting good bacteria from a healthy person's poo into a poorly person's gut. It really works!
goblet cell. A cell shaped like a wine glass that squirts out mucus.
peristalsis. Waves of muscle squeezing that push food and poo along your gut.
pili. Tiny hairs that bacteria use to hold on to things.
rectum. The very end of the gut, where poo waits until you get to a toilet.
sphincter. A ring of muscle that squeezes shut, like the drawstring on a bag.
stercobilin. The stuff that makes poo brown. It comes from old red blood cells!
Correct!
Brilliant!
Yes! Power up!
Spot on!
